scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Dutty Wine originated in Jamaica alongside iconic dancehall creations such as 'Log on' and 'Screechie'.
While several dancers claimed origin, dancehall queen Mad Michelle traced her performance of the move to a 2003 video recording.
However, the packaged visual concept of the dance emerged strongly from a Montego Bay dance group named The Attitude Girls.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Executed primarily during dancehall sessions, street parties, and international Dancehall Queen competitions, the Dutty Wine represents female athletic virtuosity, physical stamina, and personal flair within dancehall culture.
The move allows dancers to display technical speed, muscular control, and rhythmic dexterity within an intensely competitive performance setting.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The core kinetic component of the Dutty Wine involves continuous, fluid gyration, often referred to in dancehall culture as 'winding'.
The dancer initiates a rapid rotating movement of the neck, swinging their head in rhythm with the music.
Simultaneously, the dancer coordinates bird-like leg movements alongside continuous rotations of the wrists, neck, and posterior.
Watch for Neck Rotation, Dutty Wine Splits.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music for the Dutty Wine is grounded in contemporary Jamaican dancehall, driven by digital riddims designed for modern club and sound system culture.
The definitive musical backing of the movement is Tony Matterhorn's 2006 track 'Dutty Wine', composed over the high-tempo Smash riddim.
Listen for the Digital synthesizers, Electronic drum machine, Bass synthesizer, Vocal chants.
The pulse is 4/4 at about 107 beats a minute.
Modern digital dancehall sound defined by driving electronic basslines, rapid snare patterns, and high-energy vocal delivery over a continuous riddim structure.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key historical figures associated with the dance include Mad Michelle, a dancehall queen who documented early performances of the move in 2003.

The dance trio The Attitude Girls from Montego Bay consolidated the performance concept, with group member Dancehall Queen Shalara Gayle renowned for performing the fastest and longest iterations of the dance.
Following its 2006 global surge, the Dutty Wine developed regional presence within Caribbean diaspora communities across North America and the United Kingdom.
The Dutty Wine belongs to the modern lineage of Jamaican dancehall moves created in urban community contexts alongside moves like 'Log on' and 'Screechie'.

scenes.title: Common mistakes and what to avoid
narration: Avoid uncontrolled or jerky neck twisting; medical professionals warn of potential muscle trauma and ligament damage to the neck.
Teachers of this dance warn against: starting in heels when doing it for the first time
Teachers of this dance warn against: wearing long earrings that could injure your neck or hair
